prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

This is the ship of pearl, which, poets feign, Sails the unshadowed main,— The venturous bark that flings On the sweet summer wind its purpled wings In gulfs enchanted, where the Siren sings, And coral reefs lie bare, Where the cold sea-maids rise to sun their streaming hair. Its webs of living gauze no more unfurl; Wrecked is the ship of pearl! And every chambered cell, Where its dim dreaming life was wont to dwell, As the frail tenant shaped his growing shell, Before thee lies revealed,— Its irised ceiling rent, its sunless crypt unsealed! Year after year beheld the silent toil That spread his lustrous coil; Still, as the spiral grew, He left the past year’s dwelling for the new, Stole with soft step its shining archway through, Built up its idle door, Stretched in his last-found home, and knew the old no more. Thanks for the heavenly message brought by thee, Child of the wandering sea, Cast from her lap, forlorn! From thy dead lips a clearer note is born Than ever Triton blew from wreathèd horn! While on mine ear it rings, Through the deep caves of thought I hear a voice that sings:— Build thee more stately mansions, O my soul, As the swift seasons roll! Leave thy low-vaulted past! Let each new temple, nobler than the last, Shut thee from heaven with a dome more vast, Till thou at length art free, Leaving thine outgrown shell by life’s unresting sea!

outputs.L2:
Poets imagine this pearly vessel voyaging across a bright, shadowless ocean. It is a daring little craft, casting violet sails into the warm summer breeze and traveling through magical waters where Sirens sing, coral beds stand exposed, and chilly sea nymphs emerge to dry their flowing hair in the sunlight.

Now its delicate, living membranes will never spread again: the pearly ship has been destroyed. All its separate chambers, once occupied by a faint, dreamlike life while the fragile creature formed its ever-growing shell, are laid open before you. The rainbow-tinted roof is broken, and the dark inner rooms, long hidden from the sun, have been uncovered.

Each passing year witnessed the creature’s quiet labor as it enlarged its gleaming spiral. Whenever the coil expanded, it abandoned the chamber of the previous year and moved gently beneath a radiant arch into a newly made home. Then it sealed the unused entrance behind itself, settled into the latest space, and left the former dwelling forever.

Thank you, forsaken child of the roaming ocean, thrown from the sea’s embrace, for the divine lesson you bring. Though you are dead, your silent mouth conveys a purer message than any Triton ever sounded through his twisted shell-horn. As that message echoes in my hearing, a song rises through the deepest passages of my mind:

My soul, as the rapidly passing seasons turn, create increasingly magnificent homes for yourself. Abandon the cramped chambers of your former existence. Let every new sanctuary surpass the one before it, enclosing you beneath a broader and loftier dome, until you finally become free and leave your outgrown shell beside the endlessly restless sea of life.
outputs.L3:
In Oliver Wendell Holmes Sr.’s poem “The Chambered Nautilus,” the nautilus is portrayed as a magnificent “ship of pearl” sailing across an enchanted sea. Its delicate, shining shell resembles a tiny vessel moving through a mysterious and beautiful world. When the shell is broken open, however, it reveals the hidden chambers in which the creature once lived and gradually grew.

As the nautilus developed, it built a larger chamber for itself each year. It then moved into the new space and sealed off the chamber it had previously occupied. This natural process becomes a powerful symbol of progress: the creature continually outgrew its former home and left it behind in order to enter a larger one.

Although the shell is now empty and abandoned, it offers the speaker a profound spiritual lesson about growth and renewal. The nautilus’s expanding chambers represent the stages of human development, while its movement from one chamber to the next suggests that growth requires leaving old limitations behind. Inspired by this message, the speaker urges the soul to continue building “more stately mansions.” By expanding its thoughts, ideals, and spiritual capacities, the soul can move toward ever greater freedom until it finally breaks free from all earthly limitations.
outputs.L4:
In Oliver Wendell Holmes’s “The Chambered Nautilus,” the speaker reflects on the nautilus as both a natural wonder and a symbol of spiritual development. The creature inhabits a beautiful spiral shell divided into a series of chambers. As it grows, it creates larger chambers, moves into them, and seals off the smaller spaces it has outgrown. Although the shell is eventually broken and abandoned, its structure reveals the quiet, continuous process by which the nautilus has expanded its home throughout its life.

This process becomes an extended metaphor for the growth of the human soul. Each abandoned chamber represents an earlier stage of life—a former identity, belief, or limitation that was once necessary but can no longer contain the developing spirit. The nautilus does not remain confined within its old dwelling; instead, it steadily builds a larger and more spacious one. In the same way, people should not allow the habits or limitations of the past to restrict their moral and spiritual progress.

The poem’s final stanza turns the shell’s lesson into a direct command: “Build thee more stately mansions, O my soul.” The speaker urges the soul to create ever nobler inner spaces as the “swift seasons roll.” Growth therefore requires both construction and release. A person must cultivate greater wisdom, virtue, and spiritual depth while also leaving behind the “low-vaulted past.” The sealed chambers suggest that earlier experiences remain part of the soul’s history, even though it has moved beyond them.

Ultimately, the nautilus offers a vision of life as continual self-transcendence. Its expanding shell teaches that genuine development comes through repeatedly surpassing one’s former limits. This process continues until death, when the soul leaves its final physical dwelling just as the nautilus abandons its shell. The poem thus transforms a fragile object from the sea into a powerful emblem of immortality: by continually building a nobler inner life, the soul prepares itself to become free of its mortal boundaries.
